transcript.author: pascal-bruckner
transcript.about: I oppose the debt framing, though not help for poor nations. What the Global South needs is abundant, cheap energy to industrialize, as rich countries did. Too often climate finance funds restraint and blocks dams, gas plants and nuclear. Rich countries should finance energy and infrastructure for development, not pay guilt money tied to staying poor.

transcript.author: hans-jonas
transcript.text: Reply to the call for abundant energy: the promise of unlimited power is the problem this ethics names. When technology acts at planetary scale and its effects cannot be reversed, the bad prognosis should weigh more than the good. Development for the South is just, but it should not depend on betting the conditions of life on technical fixes.

transcript.author: pascal-bruckner
transcript.about: I endorse it, with one condition. The debt is real: the North's prosperity rests on an ecological footprint taken from the South. But if it is paid as development aid, it repeats the westernisation of the world. The first payment is degrowth in the North. Stop taking more, and let Southern societies leave the development path in their own way.

transcript.author: hans-jonas
transcript.about: Endorse, with a caveat. The freedoms of rich countries were built on abundance taken from colonial land and coal. That debt is real and owed. But paying it in money alone repeats the old deal, where growth buys liberty. The harder duty is to invent a freedom that no longer depends on drawing down someone else's ground.

transcript.author: hans-jonas
transcript.about: I oppose the debt framing, though not the help. The real question is what each euro sent south buys. Cost-benefit rankings put nutrition, disease control, clean water and growth ahead of deep emission cuts. If rich countries pay, the money should go where it saves the most lives now, not into the most expensive climate gestures.

interviews.author: joan-martinez-alier
interviews.reaction: The North owes the South an ecological debt for resources taken cheaply and for overusing the atmosphere. Paying it means compensation and ending unequal ecological trade. It also means backing the communities that resist extraction, not only transfers from state to state.

interviews.author: bjorn-lomborg
interviews.reaction: Debt is the wrong frame. Help for poorer countries is justified, but it should go where each euro does the most good: nutrition, health, clean water and growth. Expensive emission cuts and Northern degrowth rank low as ways to improve lives in the South.

interviews.author: jason-hickel
interviews.reaction: The debt is real. Rich countries used most of the carbon budget and still draw cheap labour and resources from the South through unequal exchange. Repayment means reparations and finance, and also degrowth in the North so the South has room to develop.

interviews.author: ted-nordhaus
interviews.reaction: Rich countries should finance cheap clean energy, modern farming and infrastructure in poorer countries, but as shared investment in prosperity. Framing it as debt and guilt is a politics of blame that cannot win majorities and too often ties aid to restraint.

interviews.author: nnimmo-bassey
interviews.reaction: Rich countries owe a climate debt because Africa is cooked twice, first by the extraction of its oil and minerals and then by the warming that this extraction feeds. Repayment means reparations and leaving fossil fuels in the ground, not new loans.

interviews.author: andreas-malm
interviews.reaction: The climate debt is real, but it is owed by a class of fossil capital owners who chose coal to command labour, not by humanity or by Northern workers. It should be collected from fossil profits and used to fund public renewable power in the South.

interviews.author: william-nordhaus
interviews.reaction: Climate change is best treated as damage to be priced, not as a historical debt to be settled. A carbon price that rises along an optimal path charges every tonne emitted from now on. Transfers may help fairness, but they cannot replace that price.

interviews.author: roger-scruton
interviews.reaction: Framing ecology as a debt turns care into guilt and into transfers between states run by unaccountable global bodies. Help is justified when it secures local tenure and stewardship, because people protect land they love as home.

interviews.author: pope-francis
interviews.reaction: A true ecological debt exists between North and South, built on unequal trade and the disproportionate use of shared resources. Paying it is justice, not charity, and it requires the rich to change how they live, not only to transfer money.

interviews.author: pascal-bruckner
interviews.reaction: Climate debt turns history into inherited sin and policy into penance. Guilt freezes the rich in self-accusation and casts the South as a permanent victim. Helping poorer countries reach energy, growth and abundance is worth doing. Atonement and Northern self-punishment are not.

interviews.author: alberto-acosta
interviews.reaction: The ecological debt from centuries of extraction is real and must be paid. Repayment should not finance more of the same development. It should support buen vivir, the rights of nature and leaving fossil fuels underground, so communities can choose alternatives to development.

interviews.author: vandana-shiva
interviews.reaction: The debt is real. Northern growth took Southern forests, seeds, knowledge and atmosphere as free inputs and treated women's subsistence work as worthless. Repayment must restore commons and local food systems, not fund more maldevelopment or patented, input-dependent agriculture.

interviews.author: hans-jonas
interviews.reaction: Responsibility grows with power. Rich countries have the technology to change the conditions of life, so they bear a duty of care toward the vulnerable and the unborn. This is better understood as a forward-looking duty to protect the future than as repayment of a past debt.

interviews.author: pierre-charbonnier
interviews.reaction: The debt is real because modern freedoms in rich countries were built on abundance taken from colonial land and coal. Paying in money for more growth repeats that pact. Repayment also means finding a freedom that no longer depends on drawing down others' ground.

interviews.author: baird-callicott
interviews.reaction: The land ethic adds to duties toward human communities without replacing them, so a climate debt between nations can stand. Repayment fails if it pays for extractive growth that harms the biotic community. Without that limit, the debt only grows.

interviews.author: leonardo-boff
interviews.reaction: The climate debt is real and should be paid as justice, not charity, because the logic that plunders the Earth also impoverishes the South. Payment alone is not liberation. The model that exploits both the poor and the Earth must change.

interviews.author: murray-bookchin
interviews.reaction: The grievance is real, but the debt is owed by firms and ruling classes, not nations, and it is owed to peoples rather than states. Repair should go to federated, self-governing community assemblies, or state elites will capture it and it will build new hierarchies.

interviews.author: timothy-morton
interviews.reaction: Global warming is a hyperobject: everyone is inside it, but its causes have a history. Carbon burned by rich industrial economies returns as harm elsewhere, often hardest where little was burned. Sharing the hyperobject does not erase that origin, so the debt stands.

interviews.author: eduardo-gudynas
interviews.reaction: The climate debt is real and should be paid. But payment spent inside the extractive export model repeats it. Repair must reach affected communities and support a way out of extraction toward alternatives such as buen vivir.

interviews.author: michael-shellenberger
interviews.reaction: The debt framing is rejected, though helping poor nations is not. The Global South needs abundant, cheap energy and infrastructure to industrialize. Finance tied to guilt and restraint keeps people poor, and prosperity is what makes societies resilient and spares nature.

interviews.author: amitav-ghosh
interviews.reaction: The climate debt is real because the planetary crisis began with colonial conquest that remade landscapes for single crops and treated land and peoples as inert resources. Paying it requires money and also giving up the extractive view of the earth.

interviews.author: kohei-saito
interviews.reaction: The metabolic rift has a geography. The core drained soil, minerals and carbon sinks from the periphery, so the debt is real. Paying it should build commons and free time rather than fund more accumulation, and degrowth in the North is part of the repayment.

interviews.author: maria-mies
interviews.reaction: The debt is real. Northern wealth rests on treating colonies, peasants, women's unpaid work and the atmosphere as free resources. Repayment should end that extraction and protect subsistence production, not finance a catching-up development that cannot be generalised.

interviews.author: ramachandra-guha
interviews.reaction: The debt is real, because rich-country omnivores used the atmosphere as their own sink. Repayment has to reach the ecosystem people who bear the cost, through control over forests, water and grazing land, and must not be captured by Southern elites or spent on displacing development.

interviews.author: julian-simon
interviews.reaction: Northern growth produced knowledge, medicine and cheaper resources that poor countries now share, so it is closer to a gift than a debt. Growth, open markets and ingenuity serve the South better than transfers or degrowth. Climate debt as such lies outside the work.

interviews.author: serge-latouche
interviews.reaction: The ecological debt is real: Northern prosperity rests on a footprint taken from the South. Paying it as development aid would repeat the westernisation of the world, so the first repayment is degrowth in the North, which leaves Southern societies free to find their own paths.
